question: When Should I Use a Custom Post Type Instead of Regular Pages?
metaDescription: When content has a repeating, structured shape (team members, case studies, listings) that benefits from its own archive, fields and templates.
shortAnswer: A custom post type makes sense when content has a genuinely repeating, structured shape — team members, case studies, property listings, recipes — that benefits from its own dedicated archive page, consistent custom fields, and its own template design, distinct from regular pages or blog posts. Using regular Pages for this kind of repeating structured content works at a small scale but becomes unwieldy and inconsistent as the content grows.

bodyHtml:
Why Structure Matters

Regular Pages are designed for unique, standalone content — an About page, a Contact page — each with its own individual purpose and typically no expectation of a shared archive or consistent structure across many similar items. A custom post type, by contrast, is built specifically for content that repeats in a structured way, giving each entry the same set of custom fields, the same template design, and a proper archive page listing them all together automatically.

Good Candidates for a Custom Post Type

  • Team members, testimonials, case studies, portfolio pieces — content that repeats in a consistent structure and benefits from a dedicated archive/listing page.
  • Property listings, events, recipes, job postings — anything with specific structured fields (a date, a price, a location) that would otherwise need to be manually formatted inconsistently within regular page content.
  • Content that needs its own URL structure or taxonomy distinct from regular pages/posts, like categorizing case studies by industry separately from the blog's own category taxonomy.
  • Content a non-technical editor needs to add repeatedly without needing to manually recreate formatting each time, which a custom post type with defined fields handles much more reliably than freeform page content.

When Regular Pages Are Still Fine

  1. A small handful of genuinely unique pages (fewer than perhaps 5-10 similar items) may not yet justify the overhead of a custom post type.
  2. Content with no real repeating structure across items doesn't benefit from the custom-fields aspect a post type provides.
  3. As content grows past a manageable handful of similar pages, migrating to a custom post type becomes worth the setup investment.
